# Glossary {#sec-appG}

Each entry gives the term as this book uses it, in a sentence or two, and the section that defines it and shows it working. The definition in the chapter is the authority, and the chapter cites the source behind it; an entry here is a reminder, not a replacement. Where the industry has a second name for the same idea, both are listed and one points to the other.

The glossary grows with the book. It holds only terms that a written chapter defines.

## A–C {#sec-appG-a}

Agent
: A loop that decides which tools to call and in what order, as distinct from the tools themselves, which are deterministic programs that can be tested on their own. See @sec-appI.

AIGER
: The exchange format for and-inverter graphs: a header of counts, then inputs, latches, outputs and AND gates as lines of literals, a literal being twice a variable's index plus one if inverted. See @sec-ch17-aig.

And-inverter graph (AIG)
: A circuit written with two-input AND gates only, inversion being a mark on an edge. Not canonical, but linear in the circuit and three clauses for each gate away from CNF. See @sec-ch17-aig.

Antecedent
: The left side of an implication in an assertion: the condition that says on which ticks the rule applies. The right side, the consequent, is what must then hold. See @sec-ch09-properties.

Assertion
: A property written in a form a tool can check, together with the instruction to check it. In this book's subset, a concurrent assertion with a clock, a reset that switches it off, and a boolean or an implication to this tick or the next. See @sec-ch09-what.

Associative array
: A SystemVerilog container indexed by a key of any type, such as an address, a string or a struct, that holds only the entries written to it. See @sec-ch05-aggregates.

Assumption
: A property the environment is expected to keep, stated about a block's inputs. In simulation it is checked like an assertion; a failure blames the stimulus, not the design. In a formal tool it is a constraint: only traces that satisfy every assumption are examined, so an assumption that is too strong proves things that are false. See @sec-ch09-where.

Assume-guarantee reasoning
: Proving a block's properties under assumptions about its neighbors, and discharging each assumption as an assertion in the neighbor's own verification. See @sec-ch09-where.

Assumption sanity
: The check that a proof's assumptions leave the design room to fail: a deep cover that time keeps passing, and a witness cover for each assertion under the final assumptions. A dead end that only some traces meet is shown only by the assertion's own witness cover. See @sec-ch19-sanity.

Back-pressure
: The receiver's use of `ready` in a valid/ready handshake to slow the sender. See @sec-ch03-pipelines.

Base case
: The half of a k-induction proof that asks for a counterexample of fewer than $k$ steps from an initial state. It is a bounded search. See @sec-ch18-induction.

Beat
: One cycle's worth of payload in a handshake: the unit the two wires arbitrate over. One message may take several beats. See @sec-ch03-pipelines.

Bin
: The unit a coverpoint counts. Each bin names a value, a set of values, or a sequence of values, and the coverage percentage is computed over bins. See @sec-ch08-bins.

Binary decision diagram (BDD)
: A graph in which each node tests one variable and has a low and a high successor, ending in the terminals 0 and 1. Ordered and reduced, it is a canonical form of a function for a fixed variable order. See @sec-ch17-bdd.

Bind
: The SystemVerilog statement that instantiates one module inside another from outside the target's source, used to attach a checker to RTL without editing it. See @sec-ch09-where.

Bit-blasting
: Reducing a formula over machine words to a propositional one by replacing each word operator with a circuit for it and encoding the circuit as clauses. See @sec-ch17-smt.

Bit-vector
: A fixed-width machine word as a solver's theory defines it: arithmetic modulo a power of two, no X or Z, and signedness carried by the operator, not the value. See @sec-ch17-smt.

Black box
: A module instance whose contents are removed from the formal model: its outputs become free inputs and its inputs are ignored. The model is an over-approximation, so a proof holds for the design and a counterexample may be spurious. See @sec-ch19-bbox.

Bound
: The number of transitions in an unrolling; bound $k$ has $k + 1$ states. Tools differ by one in what they call zero. See @sec-ch17-example.

Bounded model checking (BMC)
: Asking, for one bound at a time, whether a trace of that length from an initial state ends in a bad state, as one satisfiability question. Finding nothing up to a bound is not a proof. See @sec-ch17-example.

Btor2
: A line-based format for word-level models of sequential designs, with `state`, `init`, `next`, `bad` and `constraint` lines; the form in which this book's formal tool holds a design. See @sec-ch17-aig.

Case split
: Proving a property separately under each of several conditions, together with a completeness check that the conditions cover every reachable state. See @sec-ch19-casesplit.

Certificate
: Evidence for a verdict that a simple, independent program can check: a trace for a counterexample, an inductive invariant for a proof. See @sec-ch18-trust.

Class
: A SystemVerilog type with data members and methods. Its instances are objects, created by `new` and reached through handles. See @sec-ch05-classes.

Clause
: An *or* of literals. It is violated in exactly one way, with every literal false. See @sec-ch17-logic.

Clock
: A periodic binary signal that marks the sampling point of the sequential elements it drives, characterized by a period, a duty cycle and a phase. See *primary clock*, *derived clock* and @sec-ch03-clocks.

Clock domain
: The set of registers sampled by one clock. See @sec-ch03-clocks.

Clock domain crossing (CDC)
: A path from a register in one clock domain to a register in another. A crossing is safe only through a structure designed for it, such as a synchronizer for a control signal. See @sec-ch03-cdc.

Clocking block
: A SystemVerilog construct that names a clock and states, for each signal it lists, when the testbench reads it and when the testbench's writes land, moving those reads and writes out of the region where the design updates. See @sec-ch05-clocking.

Code coverage
: Coverage the simulator derives from the RTL itself: line, toggle, FSM state, FSM transition, conditional and branch. It measures what code was exercised, not what the plan asked for. Compare *functional coverage*; see @sec-ch08-why and @sec-ch08-code-coverage.

Combinational cloud
: The logic between registers. It has no memory, and its output is a function of its inputs alone. See @sec-ch03-rtl.

Completeness check
: The proof, required by a case split, that in every reachable state at least one of the cases holds. Without it the split proves the property only for the cases listed. See @sec-ch19-casesplit.

Completeness threshold
: A bound such that, if no counterexample of at most that many steps exists, none exists at all. See @sec-ch18-bmc.

Conflict
: In a SAT solver, a clause whose literals are all false under the current assignment. See @sec-ch17-dpll.

Conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL)
: Backtracking search that, at each conflict, derives a new clause from the reasons for the conflict, adds it to the formula and jumps back to the level where that clause first forces a value. See @sec-ch17-cdcl.

Conjunctive normal form (CNF)
: A formula written as an *and* of clauses; the input form of a SAT solver. See @sec-ch17-logic.

Constraint block
: A named set of expressions over a class's random variables, all of which `randomize()` must satisfy at once. See @sec-ch07-constraints.

Context
: The sequence of tokens a generative model sees on one call; the model's entire input. See @sec-ch34-model.

Counterexample
: A trace that a property does not permit and the design can produce; one is enough to refute the property. A formal tool reports one with its depth, the cycle in which the property fails. See @sec-ch09-what.

Counterexample to induction
: A model of the step case of an induction proof: states joined by transitions, good in all but the last, the first not required to be reachable. It shows that a property is not inductive, not that it is false. See @sec-ch18-induction.

Cover (property)
: A statement that a condition should be observed at least once. A simulator counts the ticks on which it was; a formal tool produces a trace that reaches it or proves it unreachable. Paired with every assertion to show that its antecedent can be true. See @sec-ch09-vacuity.

Covergroup
: A SystemVerilog type that holds coverpoints, crosses, options and a sampling rule. It is declared once and instantiated with `new`; a covergroup declared in a class must be constructed in that class's `new`, or it collects nothing. See @sec-ch08-covergroup.

Coverpoint
: An integral expression a covergroup samples, together with the bins its values are counted into. See @sec-ch08-bins.

Cross
: The Cartesian product of the bins of two or more coverpoints, so that combinations are counted rather than single values. See @sec-ch08-cross.

Cube
: A conjunction of literals over the state bits, standing for every state that agrees with it. See @sec-ch18-ic3.

Cut point
: An internal signal whose driving logic is disconnected in the formal model, so that the signal becomes a free input. Like a black box, it makes the model an over-approximation. See @sec-ch19-cut.

Cutoff
: A parameter size beyond which, by a theorem about a restricted class of systems, a property that holds at the cutoff holds at every size. No cutoff theorem covers parameterized RTL in general. See @sec-ch19-param.

## D–H {#sec-appG-d}

Data independence
: The property of a design that only stores and moves some data and never computes on it, compares it or branches on it. For such a design a property about one freely chosen data word stands for every word. See @sec-ch19-track.

Decomposition (property)
: Replacing an end-to-end property by a chain of local lemmas, each closer to the logic that keeps it, and proving that the end-to-end property follows from them. The lemmas are then the work, and no lemma's proof may assume the end-to-end property or a lemma whose own proof assumed it. See @sec-ch19-decomp.

Delta cycle
: VHDL's name for one pass of the simulator's loop within a timestep. This book says *iteration within a timestep*. See @sec-ch04-iteration.

Derived clock
: Any signal produced from another clock by the clock network: selected, blended, gated or shaped. See @sec-ch03-clocks.

DIMACS CNF
: The text format SAT solvers read: a header `p cnf` with the numbers of variables and clauses, then one clause to a line as signed integers ended by 0. See @sec-ch17-tseitin.

DPLL
: Search for a satisfying assignment by unit propagation, a decision when propagation stops, and backtracking on a conflict. See @sec-ch17-dpll.

Dynamic array
: A SystemVerilog array with an integer index and a size decided at run time. See @sec-ch05-aggregates.

Equisatisfiable
: Of two formulas: both satisfiable or both not. Weaker than equivalent, and what an encoding with extra variables preserves. See @sec-ch17-tseitin.

Equivalence checking
: Formal comparison of two descriptions of the same design, typically RTL and the netlist synthesized from it, to show that they compute the same function. See @sec-ch01-definitions.

Event
: Something that wakes a process or updates a value in a simulation. See @sec-ch04-model.

Evidence pointer
: The reference a derived document carries from each claim to the artifact that supports it, such as a file and line, a netlist cell, a coverage record or a run identifier. See @sec-appI-documents.

Fairness assumption
: An assumption that some condition holds infinitely often, such as `s_eventually !stall`. It removes liveness counterexamples whose loop never satisfies the condition. See @sec-ch18-liveness.

Formal verification
: Comparison of a design against properties by proof rather than by simulation. It can show that something never happens, which simulation cannot. See @sec-ch01-definitions.

Four-state
: Having four values per bit: zero, one, unknown (X) and high impedance (Z). A four-state variable can hold an unknown and propagates it. Compare *two-state*; see @sec-ch04-fourstate and @sec-ch05-types.

Frame
: In IC3, a set of states held as lemmas that contains every state reachable in at most a given number of steps. The last frame is the frontier. See @sec-ch18-ic3.

Free input
: An input of a design in a formal model: it may take any value on every tick unless an assumption constrains it. See @sec-ch09-vacuity.

Functional coverage
: Coverage a person writes from the verification plan, as covergroups and assertion cover directives, to record which behaviors the tests reached. Compare *code coverage*; see @sec-ch02-coverage and @sec-ch08.

Functional verification
: Comparison of the RTL's behavior against the specification by simulating it with a testbench. It is what "verification" means unqualified in this book. See @sec-ch01-definitions.

Generalization
: In IC3, replacing a cube that is to be blocked by a larger cube whose lemma is still inductive relative to the same frame, so that one lemma excludes many states. See @sec-ch18-ic3.

Ghost state
: Logic added for verification that reads the design and is never read by it, such as a counter or a shadow register. It does not change what the design can do. See @sec-ch19-ghost.

Helper invariant
: A property of a design's state that is proved first and then assumed, so that a later proof starts only from states that satisfy it. See @sec-ch09-example.

Handle
: A variable that names a class object. It starts `null`, and assigning one handle to another makes two names for one object, not a copy. See @sec-ch05-classes.

Handshake
: See *valid/ready handshake*.

Hierarchical contract
: Properties of a block, stated on its ports and on ghost state computed from them, proved on the block and assumed of it, as a black box, in the proof of its parent. See @sec-ch19-hier.

History variable
: Ghost state that records something about the past, so that a property can refer to an unbounded stretch of it. See @sec-ch19-history.

## I–N {#sec-appG-i}

IC3
: A proof method, also called property directed reachability (PDR), that asks only single-step queries and builds an inductive invariant one lemma at a time, in frames. See @sec-ch18-ic3.

Inductive invariant
: A set of states that contains every initial state and is closed under transitions. It proves a safety property if it contains no bad state. See @sec-ch18-reach.

Inductive strengthening
: Replacing a property that is true and not inductive by a stronger one that is, by conjoining a helper invariant. See @sec-ch18-helper.

Initial-value abstraction
: Starting a formal search from every state that satisfies an invariant instead of from reset. A proof carries back when the reset state satisfies the invariant; if the invariant is also inductive, the start set contains every reachable state. See @sec-ch19-initval.

Interface
: A named bundle of signals with its own ports and its own code, used to connect a testbench to a design. See *modport*, *virtual interface* and @sec-ch05-interfaces.

Interface class
: A class that declares only method signatures, with no data and no bodies. A class may implement several interface classes while extending at most one base class. See @sec-ch06-abstract.

Invariant
: A set of states that contains every reachable state; equivalently, a property that holds in every reachable state. See @sec-ch18-reach.

Iteration within a timestep
: One pass of the simulator's loop at a single value of simulation time. Many passes may run before time advances. Also called a *delta cycle*. See @sec-ch04-iteration.

k-induction
: A proof of a safety property by a base case, no counterexample of fewer than $k$ steps, and a step case, no $k$ good states in a row followed by a bad one. See @sec-ch18-induction.

Lasso
: A finite trace whose last state equals an earlier one: a stem, then a loop. It stands for the infinite trace that repeats the loop, and is the form of a liveness counterexample. See @sec-ch18-liveness.

Learned clause
: A clause derived by resolution at a conflict and added to the formula. It is implied by the formula, so it changes no answer; it records a fact the search will not have to find again. See @sec-ch17-cdcl.

Lemma
: In IC3, the negation of a cube: a clause read as "the design is never in these states". See @sec-ch18-ic3.

Literal
: A variable or its negation. In the AIGER format the word also names the integer that encodes a signal and its inversion. See @sec-ch17-logic.

Liveness property
: A property that says something good eventually happens. No finite prefix of a run refutes it, so a simulation cannot fail it until a bound is added. See @sec-ch09-ltl.

Liveness-to-safety
: A construction that adds a copy of the state, a save input and a flag to a design, so that a lasso violating a liveness property becomes a finite trace to a bad state. See @sec-ch18-liveness.

Memory abstraction
: Replacing a memory in a proof by one symbolic slot: a free address held constant, a shadow of the last word written there, and a contract on the boxed storage that pins what a read of the slot returns. See @sec-ch19-memabs.

Metastability
: Indecision in a flip-flop about whether its output should be zero or one, caused by a data change too close to the sampling edge. The chance that it persists falls exponentially with time but never reaches zero. See @sec-ch03-metastability.

Miter
: A circuit that feeds two circuits the same inputs and ORs together the XORs of their corresponding outputs. The two are equivalent exactly when the miter's output can never be 1. See @sec-ch17-dpll.

Modport
: A view of an interface: a list of which of its signals a module connected through that view may drive and which it may only read. See @sec-ch05-interfaces.

Monitor register
: State a checker keeps for itself, as ordinary sequential logic, so that a rule spanning several ticks becomes a condition on one. See @sec-ch09-properties.

Mutant (design)
: A copy of the design with one planted bug, used to check that some property of a set can fail. A mutant that every property passes is a gap in the set or an equivalent mutant. See @sec-ch19-mutation.

Netlist
: What synthesis produces: the design's behavior expressed as instances of library cells and the wires between them. See @sec-ch03-rtl.

Non-blocking assignment
: An assignment (`<=`) whose right side is evaluated when the statement executes and whose target is updated later in the same timestep: in the NBA region for design code, in Re-NBA for code that runs in the Reactive set. See @sec-ch04-regions.

## O–R {#sec-appG-o}

`rand`, `randc`
: Qualifiers on class members that `randomize()` assigns. A `randc` member cycles through every value of its range before repeating one. See @sec-ch07-methods.

`randomize()`
: The built-in class method that solves the class's constraints, assigns its random members, and returns 1, or returns 0 and assigns nothing when the constraints cannot be satisfied. See @sec-ch07-methods.

Object
: An instance of a class, created by `new` and reached through a handle. See @sec-ch05-classes.

Oracle input
: A free input that chooses, in a property's own logic, which cycle or which event to watch. A property proved with it holds whichever choice the engine makes. See @sec-ch19-oracle.

Over-approximation
: A changed problem that allows every behavior of the original and possibly more. It preserves proofs of safety properties; its counterexamples may be spurious. See @sec-ch19-preserve.

Over-constraint
: A set of assumptions that excludes behavior the real environment can produce. Properties proved under it are proved only for what remains; covers are the rows of a report that show it. See @sec-ch18-assume.

Parameter reduction
: Proving a design at a small parameter value in place of a large one. The result transfers only with an argument: a cutoff theorem, data independence, or an induction on the parameter. See @sec-ch19-param.

Parameterized class
: A family of classes, one per set of parameter values. Each specialization is its own type, with its own static members. See @sec-ch06-param.

Physical verification
: Comparison of a chip's layout against manufacturing rules and against its netlist. It concerns whether the chip can be built, not what it computes. See @sec-ch01-definitions.

Post-silicon validation
: Running the manufactured chip in a real system, with real software, at real speed, to find what pre-silicon verification missed. See @sec-ch01-definitions.

Primary clock
: A primary input of the design, or the output of an analog block such as a phase-locked loop treated as a black box. See @sec-ch03-clocks.

Process
: A thread of execution in a design or testbench: an `always` block, an `initial` block, or a continuous assignment. See @sec-ch04-model.

Proof core
: The part of a design that a particular proof actually used. A tighter measure of what a property set checks than the cone of influence. See @sec-ch19-core.

Proof obligation
: In IC3, a pair of a cube and a frame index: the cube must be shown unreachable within that many steps. An obligation that reaches frame 0 yields a counterexample. See @sec-ch18-ic3.

Property
: A set of traces: the ones a requirement permits. A design satisfies it when every trace it can produce is in the set. See @sec-ch09-what.

Prophecy variable
: A free value that guesses something about the future, together with a check, made when the future arrives, that the guess was right. Without care it can rule out behaviors and so hide a bug. See @sec-ch19-history.

Protocol checker role
: The parameter of a protocol checker that names which side of an interface the block under proof is on. Rules on signals the block drives are asserted; rules on signals its neighbor drives are assumed. See @sec-ch19-protocol.

Pure virtual method
: A method declared without a body in an abstract (`virtual`) class. Every concrete subclass must implement it, and the abstract class cannot itself be constructed. See @sec-ch06-abstract.

Queue
: A SystemVerilog variable-size ordered collection, its own kind of unpacked array, that grows and shrinks at either end and can be inserted into in the middle. See @sec-ch05-aggregates.

Race condition
: Two or more statements scheduled in the same timestep whose result depends on the order they run in, where the language does not fix that order. See @sec-ch04-races.

Random stability
: The resistance of random results to code changes. In SystemVerilog it comes from every thread and object having its own random number generator, so that an object's sequence depends only on the thread that constructed it and on its own earlier calls. See @sec-ch07-seeds.

Reachable state
: A state to which a sequence of transitions leads from an initial state. See @sec-ch18-reach.

Reference model
: Ghost state that computes, at some level of abstraction, what the design should do, compared with the design by assertions. See @sec-ch19-refmodel.

Region
: One of the ordered stages a SystemVerilog timestep is divided into, such as Preponed, Active, NBA, Observed, Reactive and Postponed. The order between regions may be relied on; the order between processes within one region may not. See @sec-ch04-regions.

Register
: A state element that holds a value between clock edges. See @sec-ch03-rtl.

Register-transfer level (RTL)
: A description of hardware as state elements and the combinational logic that computes each one's next value from the current ones. See @sec-ch03-rtl.

Relative induction
: A lemma is inductive relative to a frame if no initial state violates it and no transition leads from a state of the frame that satisfies it to one that does not. See @sec-ch18-ic3.

Reset domain crossing (RDC)
: A path whose source and destination registers are reset by different resets. It can cause metastability even when both registers run on one clock, so an analysis that compares only clocks cannot see it. See @sec-ch03-resets.

## S–Z {#sec-appG-s}

Safety property
: A property that says something bad never happens. Every violation shows in a finite prefix of the run, which is why a simulation can report it. See @sec-ch09-ltl.

Sample (coverage)
: One evaluation of a covergroup, in which each coverpoint's expression is read and counted into its bins. Sampling is triggered by a clocking event, a block event, or an explicit call to `sample()`. See @sec-ch08-covergroup.

Sample (generative model)
: One draw from the distribution a generative model produces. Output differs between runs unless the sampler is seeded. See @sec-ch34-model.

Sampled-value function
: `$past` and its relatives `$rose`, `$fell`, `$stable` and `$changed`: functions that compare a signal's value at this clock tick with its value at an earlier one. See @sec-ch09-properties.

SAT solver
: A program that decides whether a formula in conjunctive normal form is satisfiable, and returns a satisfying assignment when it is. See @sec-ch17-logic.

Satisfiability modulo theories (SMT)
: Satisfiability for formulas whose atoms are statements in a theory, such as comparisons of fixed-width words, not bare propositional variables. See @sec-ch17-smt.

Satisfiable
: Of a formula: true under at least one assignment. *Unsatisfiable* means true under none. See @sec-ch17-logic.

Seed
: The value that initializes a simulation's random number generation, so that a random test can be run again. See @sec-ch07-seeds.

Sequence (assertion)
: A regular expression over clock ticks, built from boolean expressions with delays and repetition; the left side of an implication in the concurrent-assertion language. See @sec-ch09-sequences.

Side condition
: An obligation that a technique creates and that must be discharged elsewhere for the technique's result to count, such as a black box's contract proved on the real block. See @sec-ch19-preserve.

Step case
: The half of a k-induction proof that asks for $k$ good states in a row followed by a bad one, starting from any state. See @sec-ch18-induction.

Structural hashing
: Keeping a table of the AND gates of a graph, keyed on their inputs, so that a gate with the same inputs is built once. See @sec-ch17-aig.

Symbolic constant
: A free input that an assumption holds constant over the whole trace. A property proved with it is proved for each of its values. See @sec-ch19-symconst.

Symbolic slot
: The one memory location, named by a symbolic constant address, that a memory abstraction keeps. See @sec-ch19-memabs.

Symmetry
: A permutation of a design's identical parts, such as channels, that maps its transitions and its initial states onto themselves, and maps the property for one part onto the property for another. A proof for one part then stands for every part it maps to. See @sec-ch19-symmetry.

Synchronizer
: A structure that carries a signal safely into another clock domain. The common two-flop synchronizer samples the signal and waits a clock period before sampling it again, trading metastability for an uncertainty of one cycle in latency. It synchronizes control, not data. See @sec-ch03-cdc.

Test (manufacturing)
: The check that a particular manufactured die came out of the fab correctly. It looks for manufacturing defects, not design errors. See @sec-ch01-definitions.

Timer abstraction
: Replacing a counter by a free expired signal and adding back, as an assumption proved on the real timer, only as much of its behavior as the property needs. See @sec-ch19-timer.

Timestep
: All the work a simulator does at one value of simulation time. Time advances only when no events remain at the current time. See @sec-ch04-model.

Token
: The unit of text a generative model reads and writes, typically a word fragment. See @sec-ch34-model.

Tool (agent tool layer)
: A deterministic program that takes a design, a testbench or a log and returns structured data, runs in continuous integration, and needs no model. See @sec-appI.

Trace
: The value of every signal at every clock tick of one run, from reset until the run stops. See @sec-ch09-what.

Transition system
: A sequential design as a model checker sees it: its initial states, the relation between a state and the next, and the states that are bad. See @sec-ch17-example.

Tseitin encoding
: The translation of a circuit to clauses that gives every wire a variable and every gate the clauses defining its output. Linear in the circuit; equisatisfiable with it, not equivalent. See @sec-ch17-tseitin.

Two-state
: Having only the values zero and one. A two-state variable cannot hold an unknown; assigning X to it stores 0. Compare *four-state*; see @sec-ch04-fourstate and @sec-ch05-types.

Two-word check
: An ordering and duplication check for a FIFO with two distinct symbolic words, each pushed at most once in order: the second must never leave before the first, and each leaves at most once. See @sec-ch19-twoword.

Under-approximation
: A changed problem that allows only some of the original's behaviors. It preserves counterexamples; its proofs say nothing about the behaviors left out. See @sec-ch19-preserve.

Undetermined
: A formal tool's report that it neither proved nor refuted a property within its limits. It says nothing about the design. See @sec-ch09-formal.

Unique-states constraint
: The requirement that the states of an induction step case be pairwise different, also called the simple-path constraint. With it k-induction is complete on finite systems. See @sec-ch18-induction.

Unit propagation
: The inference that a clause with all literals false but one, and that one unassigned, forces its last literal true; repeated until nothing is forced or a clause is violated. See @sec-ch17-dpll.

Unknown (X)
: A simulator's statement that it does not know which value a bit has. It is not a value hardware can hold. See @sec-ch04-fourstate.

Unreachable (cover)
: A formal tool's proof that no trace of the design, under the assumptions in force, makes a cover's condition true. See @sec-ch09-vacuity.

Unrolling
: Copying a design's combinational logic once for each cycle and connecting each copy's next-state outputs to the next copy's state inputs, so that a question about $k$ cycles is one formula. See @sec-ch17-example.

Vacuous pass
: A pass of an assertion whose antecedent was never true, so that nothing was checked; in a formal tool, a proof of that kind. Detected by a cover of the antecedent that reads zero or is unreachable. See @sec-ch09-vacuity.

Valid (formula)
: True under every assignment. A formula is valid exactly when its negation is unsatisfiable. See @sec-ch17-logic.

Valid/ready handshake
: A two-wire contract in which the sender raises `valid` to offer a beat and the receiver raises `ready` to accept one. The beat transfers only in a cycle where both are high. See @sec-ch03-pipelines.

Validation
: The question of whether the specification is the right one for the product and the world it must work in. Compare *verification* and *test*; see @sec-ch01-definitions.

Variable order
: The order in which a binary decision diagram tests its variables. It fixes the diagram's size, which for an adder's carry is linear in one order and exponential in another. See @sec-ch17-bdd.

Verification
: The question of whether the design does what the specification says, and nothing else, answered with evidence: executed tests, coverage data and proofs. See @sec-ch01-definitions.

Verification plan
: The list of every behavior a design must have, each paired with how it will be exercised, checked and measured, and what will count as done. It is written from the specification, before the testbench. See @sec-ch02-what.

Virtual interface
: A class variable that holds a handle to an interface instance, so that class-based testbench code can drive and sample the design's wires. Like any variable it starts null. See @sec-ch05-interfaces.

Virtual method
: A method dispatched on the run-time class of the object rather than the declared class of the handle, so a call through a base handle runs the most-derived override. See @sec-ch06-virtual.

Witness cover
: A cover of the situation an assertion is about, at least its antecedent. An assertion proved while its witness is unreachable holds vacuously. See @sec-ch18-cover.
